articles.title: Man turns Robinhood-AMC feud into $2 million gain in 12 hours
articles.summary: A smart trader takes advantage of the Robinhood-AMC feud.
articles.body:
A crypto trader saw an unrealized gain of over $2 million in less than 12 hours by capitalizing on the controversy surrounding Robinhood Markets (Nasdaq: HOOD) and AMC Entertainment Holdings (NYSE: AMC).

As reported earlier , the two companies recently got involved in a major controversy.

Robinhood is an e-brokerage platform that offers equity, crypto, and stock tokens. A tokenized stock or a stock token is a digital token created on a blockchain that tracks the price of a publicly listed company's stock. It is only a synthetic version of a stock, with no official relation to the company publicly listed on a stock exchange.

On Sep. 3, AMC CEO Adam Aron criticized Robinhood for offering a tokenized version of the AMC stock without registering under U.S. securities laws and threatened legal action if it didn't stop trading the AMC stock token.

Robinhood didn't back down, as its chief legal officer, Dan Gallagher, said the firm is aware of the U.S. securities laws and won't stop offering the AMC token, daring Aron to send his lawyers.

The controversy birthed a meme coin called "A Meme Coin (AMC)" the same day.

A meme coin is a cryptocurrency inspired by internet memes, viral trends, or pop culture. Unlike Bitcoin (BTC) or Ethereum (ETH), meme coins usually have no real-world utility. Their value relies entirely on online hype, social media buzz, and community excitement.

A Meme Coin's acronym, AMC, pokes fun at the entertainment giant's viral feud with Robinhood. The coin rallied from $0.00008571 to $0.1509 within a few hours, a surge of approximately 176,000%.

Crypto trader sees over $2 million paper gain on MEME rally

As per the onchain analytics platform Lookonchain , a crypto trader bought 6.11 million MEME for $2,972 when the meme coin was just launched.

As MEME rallied, the trader sold 750,000 coins for $85,300. But they are still holding 15.36 million MEME with an unrealized gain of $2.03 million, Lookonchain said on Sep. 4 at 3:20 AM ET.

The meme coin has since crashed and was trading at $0.03136 at the time of writing.

This story was originally published by TheStreet on Sep 5, 2026, where it first appeared in the MARKETS section. Add TheStreet as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

articles.title: Stablecoins Won't Scale Without Banks
articles.summary: With a growing number of institutions exploring stablecoins, the bottleneck is regulated infrastructure they can trust.
articles.body:
Stablecoins were supposed to route around the banking system. Instead, the companies scaling them are building deeper into it than anyone predicted.

Stripe paid $1.1 billion for Bridge , whose core product is orchestrating banks. Citi is launching crypto custody . Standard Chartered is testing stablecoin settlement in Singapore. One by one, the operators moving institutional volume keep landing on the same architecture.

An enterprise cross-border payment has three legs. The payer's money moves in local currency over local rails—a Brazilian importer paying in BRL via Pix. The payee receives local currency on their end—the supplier collecting dollars in their account.

Between them sits the middle leg: getting value across the border from one institution to the other. That leg used to run through correspondent banking, SWIFT messages hopping between intermediary banks, each holding accounts with the next, each adding a day and a fee. When both institutions accept a stablecoin, that leg settles on-chain in seconds. Banks still own the other two.

That is the division of labor. Stablecoins settle the middle leg. Every flow still begins and ends in fiat, and that is where banks are non-negotiable: the entry point, the compliance anchor, and the local rails in every market a payment touches. The companies scaling on stablecoin rails built into the banking system, corridor by corridor.

Every enterprise payment flow begins in a bank account. Payroll, vendor invoices, customer revenue, and capital distributions live in fiat, they move through regulated financial infrastructure, and the companies sending and receiving them keep that infrastructure regardless of what a payment provider prefers.

The scale of the gap makes the point concrete. The cross-border payments market reached $208 trillion in 2025, according to FXC Intelligence. Genuine stablecoin payments ran at roughly $390 billion annualized as of late 2025, per McKinsey and Artemis, which works out to about 0.02% of global payment volume across both cross-border and domestic flows. The headline figures of $30 trillion or more in annual stablecoin "volume" mostly reflect bots, exchange flows, and automated trading rather than payments. A hedge fund treasury desk, an enterprise running payroll across thirty countries, and an exchange settling institutional withdrawals all begin in fiat.

The question these operators ask is which banking infrastructure connects reliably to which settlement rails, and who built it with enough depth to hold at institutional volume. Most stablecoin companies struggle to answer.
